newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman's $6 bln gas export project -- an overview.
newsitem.headline: Oman's $6 bln gas export project -- an overview.

text.p: Oman has put into place this month the main contracts for a $6 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project which will shake-up the Gulf Arab state's oil-dependent economy from the year 2000.
An overview of the internationally-backed project follows.
PROJECT PARAMETERS

Natural gas from Barik, Saih Rawl and Saih Nihayda fields in central Oman will be developed and piped to a two-train 6.6 million tonnes a year capacity liquefaction plant at Al Ghalilah, 200 km (125 mile) southeast of Muscat.
LNG from the plant will be exported by special sea-going tankers to Asian power utilities, mainly in South Korea.
The liquefaction plant is scheduled for completion in December 1999, allowing the first export cargo to Korea Gas Corporation (KOGAS) in the first quarter of the year 2000.
ECONOMIC IMPACT
Oman has banked on the LNG scheme, the biggest project in the country, to diversify its economy and increase employment levels among Omanis.

Omani officials say exports will boost the country's oil revenue (1.02 billion Omani rials Jan-Aug 1996) by 18 percent and contribute 10 percent to GDP when fully running. The government will also benefit from the sales of some 80,000 barrels per day (bpd) of light oil known as condensate.
FOREIGN UPSTREAM ROLE

Financing and operating the gas fields necessary for the project is being carried out by Petroleum Development Oman (PDO), the country's largest oil operator. PDO is 60 percent owned by the Oman government. Royal Dutch/Shell has 34 percent, Total SA four percent and Partex two percent.
The gas is 100 percent owned by the Oman government and operated on its behalf by PDO under a 25-year lease.
Financing the $1.4 billion upstream development is being undertaken by PDO's three foreign shareholders.

"The government would pay the investment value to the Private Shareholders as of 2001 through 2006 from the income earned from selling gas and condensate associated with natural gas," according to Oman's Ministry of National Economy.
Engineering contracts to develop upstream facilities are in the process of being awarded.
FOREIGN DOWNSTREAM ROLE
Oman LNG Limited Liability Company (LLC) was set up by Royal Decree to handle the downstream element of the gas project -- the liquefaction plant, transportation and sales of LNG.
Oman LNG is 51 percent owned by the Omani government.
Shell has 30 percent Total SA 5.54 percent, Partex two percent, Mitsubishi 2.77 percent, Mitsui and Co also 2.77 percent, ITOCHU Corp 0.92 percent.
South Korean Gas Corp (KOGAS) -- comprising Yukong, Hyundai, Daewoo and Samsung -- holds the remaining five percent.
Limited recourse financing for the downstream work is being arranged and is planned to be in place in the middle of 1997.
Banks and export credit agencies were selected on November 17 arrange $2 billion of loans for downstream work.
Seven banks arranging the downstream loan are ABN-Ambro, National Westminister Bank Plc, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, Citibank, Banque Indosuez, Korea Exchange Bank and Gulf International Bank.
UK, U.S., Dutch and Italian export agencies are involved.
Oman LNG anticipates raising 80 percent of its financing requirements through loans from commercial banks. The rest of the requirement comes from equity.

The liquefaction plant will be built by Japan's Chiyoda and Foster Wheeler Corp under a $1 billion engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract signed on November 14. Two Omani firms will also work on the plant.
Oman's Sultan Qaboos bin Said laid the cornerstone for the $1 billion LNG plant on November 16.
GAS CUSTOMERS

Oman LNG LLC has a definite sales and purchase agreement for gas supplies to KOGAS. Under the 25-year supply agreement the south Korean utility will initially lift two million tonnes in 2000 rising to a plateau annual rate of 4.1 million tonnes.
A heads of agreement has been signed with Petroleum Authority of Thailand for supply of up to an annual 2.2 million tonnes of Omani LNG from 2003.
Talks with Japanese power utilities are now underway to meet potential short gap between Korean and Thai contract start ups.
OMANI GAS RESERVES

Oman's proven gas reserves stand at 17 trillion cubic feet. "Expected" reserves are 25 trillion cubic feet and could rise to as much as 40 trillion cubic feet by the turn of the decade. Omani crude output runs at 900,000 bpd.
($1= 0.38 Omani rial)
